tagline: Hills, forests and the Mohican country where Chapman tended apple nurseries
intro: The Johnny Appleseed Historic Byway follows more than 30 miles along State Route 39, through the country associated with John Chapman’s nursery work. Near Lucas, the setting includes hills and forests, with Charles Mill Lake to the east and Pleasant Hill Lake to the south. Ohio’s Department of Transportation promotes the byway for Chapman’s landholdings and nurseries, alongside sites of Native American culture and early settlements.

Chapman’s work depended on more than planting seeds. He fenced his nurseries against animals, left neighbors to sell the trees on shares, and returned every year or two to tend them. Many nurseries were in the Mohican River area, including Mansfield, Lucas, Perrysville and Loudonville.

Start in Mansfield, then follow the SR 39 corridor southeast toward Lucas. Malabar Farm lies near Lucas, while Charles Mill Lake lies near Mifflin. Farther southeast, Perrysville and Loudonville stand along the Black Fork of the Mohican River.

moments.title: Mansfield Square
moments.text: Mansfield’s public square, now Central Park, began as the center of the town’s 1808 plan. Two blockhouses were erected here during the War of 1812. After the war, one housed Richland County’s courthouse and jail until 1816, then served as a school. The blockhouse moved to South Park in 1929. A different marker of travel history stands in Central Park: a concrete Lincoln Highway post, originally erected on Park Avenue West in 1928. The post bears an Abraham Lincoln profile medallion, a reminder of the cross-country highway that reached Mansfield in 1913.
moments.notice: Look for the Lincoln Highway post on Park Avenue’s center divider in Central Park.

moments.title: Malabar Farm State Park
moments.text: Louis Bromfield changed the shapes of fields at Malabar Farm to follow the land and discourage erosion. The author bought a Pleasant Valley farm in 1938, then added neighboring farms in 1940 and 1941. With expertise and labor from the Soil Conservation Service and Civilian Conservation Corps, he rehabilitated the land and promoted soil-conserving techniques. His experiments included contour plowing, green manures and composting with manure from the farm’s livestock. The farm became a state park in 1976. Its main barn is a replacement: after a 1993 fire, Timber Framers Guild volunteers raised a new barn resembling the original in 1994.

moments.title: Copus Monument
moments.text: The Copus Monument belongs to the history of violence near the Black Fork during the War of 1812. After Native Americans were forcibly removed from Greentown, attacks killed members of the Zimmer family and their neighbor Martin Ruffner. Several days later, James Copus and three militiamen were killed defending his home and family. A monument on Route 603 near Charles Mill Dam commemorates these events, while a marker in the lake’s day-use area recounts the wartime violence.
